title: No Gangsters, No Conspiracies. Just the Mishras. Gullak Just Became the First Hindi Show Ever to Hit Five Seasons.
excerpt: TVF's quiet middle-class miracle is back on SonyLIV with a new Annu, a Wi-Fi router that displaces the piggy bank, and a diaspora fanbase that watches it like a phone call home.
body:
The season opens not with a gunshot or a body, but with paint tubs. Rollers, scrapers, a long-delayed whitewash scattered across the front ledge of Mishra Niwas. A Wi-Fi router arrives and gets installed because Annu now sits through online meetings — and in doing so, it nudges the beloved earthen gullak, the piggy-bank narrator, out of its old corner. That single image tells you everything about where this show is in 2026: technology and tradition, elbowing each other for space on the same shelf.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=yhxf4SYE1gg

At a moment when Indian streaming is drowning in gangland sagas and grim, blue-tinted thrillers, Gullak remains the gentle rebel. No conspiracies. No high-stakes suspense. Just a family, a modest house in a nameless North Indian town, and the countless small moments that make up a middle-class life. And now it has done something no Hindi original ever has — reached a fifth season.

"With every season, Gullak has grown closer to audiences because the Mishras feel like a family we all know." — Vijay Koshy, President, TVF

The Mishras have never felt like fictional characters. They feel like people you're related to. The arguments over electricity bills, the passive-aggressive negotiations over whose turn it is to do what, the way love hides under scolding and tired jokes after a long day — it's all drawn from lived experience, and it lands differently when you're watching it 8,000 miles from home.

Season 5 hands the family some real upheaval. Annu Mishra — now played by Anant V. Joshi, stepping in for Vaibhav Raj Gupta — moves into a rented flat with friends, chasing a little independence from his ever-demanding household. Aman returns quieter, carrying secrets of his own, and discovers a side hustle as an online astrologer, dispensing questionable advice and inevitably landing himself in trouble. Shanti (the wonderful Geetanjali Kulkarni) unexpectedly tastes a little fame, thanks to the online popularity of "Bittu Ki Mummy" in a world suddenly obsessed with being seen. And Santosh begins quietly dreaming of buying a new house, loan and all — the most middle-class ambition there is.

Recasting the eldest son is the kind of move that can sink a beloved show. The fact that it doesn't is a quiet testament to how sturdy this world is. Joshi doesn't try to imitate; he inherits. And the ensemble around him — Jameel Khan as the perpetually exasperated Santosh, Harsh Mayar, Sunita Rajwar's scene-stealing Bittu Ki Mummy, Helly Shah — slots back together like a family that never actually left.

The critics have largely fallen for it again. Filmfare gave it 3.5 stars, calling it "a warm return to the Mishra household." Filmibeat went higher at 4 out of 5, praising the "same warmth with new flavours." Not everyone's sold — The Hollywood Reporter India confessed to yawning through the curated whimsy, arguing the show has grown a little too comfortable, a little too insulated from the country it claims to portray. But even that grumpiness is a kind of compliment: you only get this annoyed at family.

What's changed is the texture. This season runs seven episodes instead of the old five, and there's a broader arc of evolution stitching them together. Everyone is inching forward, caught in what the show frames beautifully as the transition between "a wrinkled yesterday and a shapeless tomorrow." The renovation isn't just set design — it's the whole thesis. Middle-class families accept the dust and the noise because someone promised them comfort at the end of it.

Where to watch (diaspora edition): All seven episodes of Gullak Season 5 are streaming now on SonyLIV, which carries international subscriptions across the US, UK, and Canada. For NRIs, the show has always been less of a binge and more of a ritual — the closest thing streaming has to calling your parents on a Sunday. If you've never started, the good news is the seasons stand largely on their own; the bad news is you'll want all five anyway.

In an industry obsessed with universe-building and ₹300-crore spectacles, there's something almost radical about a show that still believes a family arguing over a Wi-Fi router is worth your time. Five seasons in, Gullak isn't keeping up with the times. It's reminding us what they cost.
